title: 190 Using two-dimensional facial images of Hereford crossbred cattle as a source of computable trait for facial patterns: from images to biological trait
content:
Abstract
Crossbred beef cattle are popular in commercial production due to the benefit of heterosis. However, many crossbred cattle exhibit a variety of random facial patterns, which cause a lack of uniformity in the herd. In Hereford cross cattle, the mottle-faced (MF) pattern arises, which is variable color pigmented areas in the expected white face (WF) seen in Herefords. The MF pattern in Hereford crosses, as well as similar crosses with white-faced breeds, vary widely in shape and size. The aim of this study is to detect, segment, classify and measure the MF pattern in Hereford-cross cattle using deep learning and computer vision approaches. For this purpose, we randomly selected 1,021 face images from a dataset of Hereford-crossed cattle 2-D facial images (n = 4,257) from seven states in the USA and regions of South Africa. In data preparation, the animal’s face was first labelled in each image using standalone LabelMe tool (5.5.0) for annotation purposes. Then a Mask R-CNN (Mask Region-Based Convolutional Neural Network) model, built in Python (3.9.0) with machine learning library of TensorFlow (2.10.0), was used to train and predict face segmentation and a MobileNet model was used for binary classification of MF or WF. The thresholding function of OpenCV measured the amount of pigmentation relative to the whole face area in the classified image and converted this subjective trait to a computable trait. The Mask R-CNN model successfully segmented the face of cattle and achieved a mean Average Precision of 1.0 at an Intersection over Union value of 0.50. The MobileNet classification model reached an accuracy of 0.81. These models and thresholding function recognized and quantified the facial patterns; this pipeline will be expanded by using imageomics principles to explore the biological phenomenon behind these patterns. This work will also be a valuable addition to ongoing work in precision livestock farming and breed identification.
